chapter.blurb: The meaning of citizenship, constitutional provisions, the Citizenship Act 1955, and overseas citizenship of India.

concepts.name: Meaning and significance of citizenship
concepts.description: Citizens and aliens, friendly and enemy aliens, and the rights and duties of citizens.
concepts.idea: Citizens are full members of the State with civil and political rights; aliens enjoy fewer rights.
concepts.rule: India has two kinds of people: citizens and aliens. Citizens are full members of the Indian State and owe it allegiance, enjoying all civil and political rights. Aliens are citizens of another state and do not enjoy all these rights. They are friendly aliens (subjects of countries with cordial relations with India) or enemy aliens (subjects of a country at war with India), who enjoy fewer rights, for example no protection against arrest and detention under Article 22. Rights available only to citizens include protection from discrimination (Article 15), equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16), the freedoms of Article 19, cultural and educational rights (Articles 29 and 30), the right to vote in Lok Sabha and state assembly elections, the right to contest, and eligibility for offices such as President, Vice-President, judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, Governors, Attorney General and Advocates General. Citizens also owe duties such as paying taxes, respecting the flag and anthem and defending the country. In India both natural-born and naturalised citizens can be President, whereas in the USA only a citizen by birth can.
concepts.example: A naturalised citizen can be President of India but not of the USA.

concepts.name: Single citizenship and its exceptions
concepts.description: Why India has one citizenship and the exceptions in employment, benefits, tribal areas and the former J&K.
concepts.idea: India has only one Indian citizenship, with a few exceptions to equal treatment.
concepts.rule: Though India is a federation, it has only single citizenship; citizens owe allegiance to the Union and there is no state citizenship. The USA and Australia have double citizenship. In the USA a person is a citizen of the nation and of a state and enjoys two sets of rights, which allows states to discriminate in favour of their own citizens in voting, offices and professions. India avoids this. Exceptions: (1) Article 16 lets Parliament prescribe residence as a condition for certain jobs; the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957 allowed residence requirements for non-Gazetted posts in Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur and Tripura, and it expired in 1974 except for Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. (2) Article 15 bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth but not residence, so a state may give concessions to its residents such as education fee concessions. (3) Freedom of movement and residence under Article 19 is subject to protection of Scheduled Tribes, restricting outsiders in tribal areas. (4) Till 2019 the legislature of Jammu and Kashmir could define permanent residents and confer special rights under Article 35A, inserted by the 1954 Order under Article 370; the 2019 Order ended this. India, like Canada, has single citizenship to promote fraternity.
concepts.example: Article 35A was inserted by a presidential order in 1954 under Article 370.

concepts.name: Constitutional provisions: who became citizens on 26 January 1950
concepts.description: Articles 5 to 8 and the four categories of persons who became citizens at commencement.
concepts.idea: Part II identifies four categories of persons who became citizens at commencement.
concepts.rule: The Constitution deals with citizenship in Articles 5 to 11 of Part II, but only identifies persons who became citizens on 26 January 1950; it leaves later acquisition and loss to Parliament. Four categories became citizens. (1) A person domiciled in India who was born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for five years before commencement. (2) A person who migrated to India from Pakistan if he or a parent or grandparent was born in undivided India and, if he came before 19 July 1948, was ordinarily resident since migration; if on or after 19 July 1948, he was registered as a citizen after six months' residence before application. (3) A person who migrated to Pakistan from India after 1 March 1947 but returned for resettlement, if registered after six months' residence. (4) A person of Indian origin (he, a parent or a grandparent born in undivided India) ordinarily residing outside India, registered by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
concepts.example: The four categories cover people domiciled in India, migrants from Pakistan, returned migrants and persons of Indian origin abroad.

concepts.name: Other constitutional provisions and the Citizenship Act 1955
concepts.description: Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship, continuation of citizenship, Parliament's power and the Act of 1955.
concepts.idea: Parliament's Citizenship Act 1955 governs acquisition and loss after 1950; foreign citizenship voluntarily acquired ends Indian citizenship.
concepts.rule: Further provisions: no person is a citizen if he has voluntarily acquired foreign citizenship (Article 9); every person who is or is deemed a citizen continues as such subject to Parliament's law; and Parliament may make provisions on acquisition and termination and all other matters of citizenship. The Citizenship Act (1955) provides for acquisition and loss after the Constitution began, and has been amended several times. It originally provided for Commonwealth citizenship, repealed by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003. The Constitution forbids dual citizenship or dual nationality (Article 9). The Act prescribes five ways of acquiring citizenship (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory) and three ways of losing it (renunciation, termination and deprivation).
concepts.example: The Citizenship Act was passed in 1955.

concepts.name: Acquisition of citizenship by birth and by descent
concepts.description: The rules by date for citizenship by birth in India and by descent when born abroad.
concepts.idea: Birth rules tightened over time from 1950 to 2004, and descent needs registration of birth at a consulate.
concepts.rule: By birth: a person born in India on or after 26 January 1950 but before 1 July 1987 is a citizen irrespective of the parents' nationality. Born on or after 1 July 1987 but before 3 December 2004, he is a citizen only if either parent is a citizen at his birth. Born on or after 3 December 2004, he is a citizen only if both parents are citizens, or one is a citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant. Children of foreign diplomats and enemy aliens cannot get citizenship by birth. By descent: born abroad on or after 26 January 1950 but before 10 December 1992, a person is a citizen if his father was a citizen at his birth; born abroad on or after 10 December 1992, if either parent was a citizen. From 3 December 2004 birth abroad gives citizenship by descent only if registered at an Indian consulate within one year (or with the Centre's permission later), with an undertaking that the minor does not hold another country's passport. A minor citizen by descent who is a citizen of another country ceases to be a citizen if he does not renounce the other citizenship within six months of attaining full age.
concepts.example: Since 2004, at least one parent must be a citizen and the other not an illegal migrant for birth in India to give citizenship.

concepts.name: Acquisition by registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory
concepts.description: Categories for registration, conditions for naturalisation, and citizenship on annexation of territory.
concepts.idea: Registration, naturalisation and incorporation give citizenship to persons with a link to India or long residence.
concepts.rule: By registration the Central Government may register persons (not illegal migrants) such as: persons of Indian origin resident in India for seven years; persons of Indian origin resident outside undivided India; persons married to citizens and resident seven years; minor children of citizens; adults whose parents are registered citizens; adults who, or whose parent, were earlier citizens of independent India and resident twelve months; and adult OCI cardholders for five years resident twelve months. A person of Indian origin is one who, or a parent of whom, was born in undivided India or in territory that became part of India after 15 August 1947. All must take an oath of allegiance. By naturalisation, the Centre grants a certificate if the person is not a subject of a country that bars Indians from naturalisation, undertakes to renounce other citizenship, resided in India twelve months before applying and eleven of the previous fourteen years (the 2019 Act reduces this to five years for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh or Pakistan), is of good character, knows an Eighth Schedule language and intends to reside in India. Conditions may be waived for distinguished service to science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace or human progress. By incorporation of territory the Government specifies who becomes a citizen when a foreign territory joins India, as in the Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order 1962.
concepts.example: The Citizenship (Pondicherry) Order was issued in 1962.

concepts.name: Special provisions: Assam Accord and Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019
concepts.description: Persons covered by the Assam Accord and migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
concepts.idea: The 1985 amendment and the 2019 Act added special routes to citizenship.
concepts.rule: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 1985 added special provisions for persons covered by the Assam Accord. Persons of Indian origin who came to Assam before 1 January 1966 from Bangladesh and have resided there since are deemed citizens from 1 January 1966. Those who came on or after 1 January 1966 but before 25 March 1971, and are detected as foreigners, must register and are deemed citizens after ten years from detection, and in the meantime have the rights and obligations of citizens except the right to vote. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2019 covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh or Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 and were exempted from penal consequences of the Passport (Entry into India) Act 1920 and the Foreigners Act 1946. They may get registration or naturalisation and are deemed citizens from their date of entry, and pending proceedings on illegal migration abate. It does not apply to Sixth Schedule tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura or the Inner Line areas. In 2015 they were exempted from penal consequences and in 2016 made eligible for long term visas. The 2019 Act came into force on 10 January 2020.

concepts.name: Loss of citizenship: renunciation, termination and deprivation
concepts.description: The three ways of losing Indian citizenship and their conditions.
concepts.idea: Citizenship can be lost by renunciation, automatic termination or compulsory deprivation.
concepts.rule: Renunciation: an adult of full capacity can declare renouncing citizenship and ceases to be a citizen on registration of the declaration, except that registration is withheld during a war in which India is engaged. When a person renounces, his minor children also lose citizenship but may resume it within one year of attaining eighteen. Termination: if a citizen voluntarily acquires another country's citizenship (consciously, knowingly and without duress) his Indian citizenship automatically ends, but not during a war in which India is engaged. Deprivation: compulsory termination by the Central Government if the citizen obtained citizenship by fraud, showed disloyalty to the Constitution, unlawfully traded or communicated with the enemy during a war, was imprisoned in any country for two years within five years after registration or naturalisation, or has been ordinarily resident outside India for seven years continuously.

concepts.name: Overseas citizenship: Singhvi Committee and the Amendment Acts of 2003, 2005 and 2015
concepts.description: The Diaspora committee, PIO and OCI schemes and their merger into the OCI cardholder scheme.
concepts.idea: OCI is not dual citizenship; the 2015 Act merged the PIO and OCI schemes.
concepts.rule: In September 2000 the Government set up a High Level Committee on the Indian Diaspora under L.M. Singhvi, which reported in January 2002 and recommended dual citizenship for Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) of specified countries. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2003 provided Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) for PIOs of 16 specified countries other than Pakistan and Bangladesh and removed Commonwealth citizenship. The 2005 Act extended it to PIOs of all countries except Pakistan and Bangladesh whose home countries allow dual citizenship. OCI is not actually dual citizenship because the Constitution forbids dual citizenship (Article 9). The PIO card scheme began on 19 August 2002 and the OCI card scheme on 2 December 2005; the two ran together causing confusion. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act 2015 merged them into the 'Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder' scheme; the PIO scheme was rescinded from 9 January 2015 and existing PIO cardholders were deemed OCI cardholders from that date.

concepts.name: OCI cardholders: registration, rights, renunciation and cancellation
concepts.description: Who may be registered as OCI cardholders, the rights denied to them and grounds of cancellation.
concepts.idea: OCI cardholders get long-term links to India but not political rights or public employment.
concepts.rule: The Central Government may register as OCI cardholder an adult who is a foreign citizen but was a citizen of India at or after commencement, or was eligible then, or belonged to territory that joined India after 15 August 1947, or is a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a person; minor children of these; a minor whose both or one parents are Indian citizens; and the foreign-origin spouse of an Indian citizen or OCI cardholder whose marriage has subsisted for at least two continuous years. Those with parents, grandparents or great-grandparents who were citizens of Pakistan, Bangladesh or another specified country are ineligible. An OCI cardholder cannot claim equality in public employment (Article 16), be President (Article 58), Vice-President (Article 66), a Supreme Court judge (Article 124) or High Court judge (Article 217), be registered as a voter, be a member of Parliament or a state legislature, or be appointed to public services except as the Centre specifies. A cardholder may renounce the card; the foreign spouse and minor children then also cease to be OCI cardholders. The Centre may cancel registration for fraud, disaffection towards the Constitution, trading with the enemy in war, two years' imprisonment within five years, violation of the Act or other specified laws (added in 2019), interests of sovereignty, security or public interest, or dissolution of the marriage or a second marriage during it. A reasonable opportunity of being heard must be given (2019).
